proofs.proof_tex:
Let \(\mathsf K\) denote the Markov kernel that maps the observed sample to the released interval \(\widetilde C_n\).  We construct two pairs of laws, with a common null law, and then convert indistinguishability of each pair into a lower bound for the expected interval length.

First construct a smooth bump without changing the support of the outcomes.  Define
\[
 b(t)=
 \begin{cases}
  \exp\{-1/(1-t^2)\},& |t|<1,\\
  0,& |t|\ge 1,
 \end{cases}
 \qquad
 \varphi(z)=b(0)^{-d}\prod_{j=1}^d b(z_j).
\]
Repeated differentiation on \((-1,1)\), together with the fact that \(s^{-M}e^{-1/s}\to0\) as \(s\downarrow0\) for every finite \(M\), shows that \(b\), and hence \(\varphi\), is \(C^\infty\).  Moreover, \(\varphi\ge0\), \(\varphi(0)=1\), and \(\varphi\) is supported on \([-1,1]^d\).

Put
\[
 p_* = \min\{1/4,L_\mu/2\}>0.
\]
Let \(\ell=\lfloor\gamma\rfloor\) and \(\sigma=\gamma-\ell\).  There is a finite constant \(C_\varphi\), depending only on \((\varphi,\gamma,d)\), with the following scaling property.  For every multi-index \(u\) with \(|u|\le\ell\),
\[
 \left\|D^u\{h^\gamma\varphi((\,cdot-x_0)/h)\}\right\|_\infty
 =h^{\gamma-|u|}\|D^u\varphi\|_\infty
 \le \|D^u\varphi\|_\infty,
\]
because \(0<h\le r_0\le1/4\).  If \(0<\sigma<1\) and \(|u|=\ell\), then
\[
 \left[D^u\{h^\gamma\varphi((\,\cdot-x_0)/h)\}\right]_{\sigma}
 =h^{\gamma-\ell-\sigma}[D^u\varphi]_{\sigma}
 =[D^u\varphi]_{\sigma}.
\]
For \(\sigma=0\), the derivative bounds in the preceding display are the required integer-order bounds.  Thus the relevant isotropic H\"older norm is at most \(C_\varphi\), uniformly over \(0<h\le r_0\).  Choose a fixed \(a_*>0\) so small that
\[
 a_*C_\varphi\le L_\tau,
 \qquad
 a_*\|\varphi\|_\infty\le p_*/2,
\]
and define
\[
 g_h(x)=a_*h^\gamma\varphi((x-x_0)/h).
\]
The boundary condition \(x_0\in[r_0,1-r_0]^d\) and \(h\le r_0\) imply that the support of \(g_h\) lies in \(\mathcal X\).  The displays above prove, rather than assume, that
\[
 g_h\in\mathcal H^\gamma(L_\tau;\mathcal X),
 \qquad 0\le g_h\le p_*/2.
\tag{1}
\]

We next define full-data laws \(Q_0\) and \(Q_h\).  Under both laws, \(X\) is uniform on \(\mathcal X\), and, conditional on \(X=x\), \(A\) is Bernoulli with success probability \(1/2\) and is independent of \((Y(0),Y(1))\).  Under \(Q_0\), conditional on \(X=x\), the two potential outcomes are independent Bernoulli variables with common mean \(p_*\).  Under \(Q_h\), they are conditionally independent Bernoulli variables with respective means
\[
 \mathbb E_{Q_h}[Y(0)\mid X=x]=p_* ,
 \qquad
 \mathbb E_{Q_h}[Y(1)\mid X=x]=p_*+g_h(x).
\tag{2}
\]
Finally set \(Y=AY(1)+(1-A)Y(0)\).

We verify membership in the frozen full class condition by condition.  Equation (2) and the last construction satisfy Assumption \texttt{ass:consistency}; conditional generation of \(A\) satisfies Assumption \texttt{ass:ignorability}.  Both potential outcomes take values in the common support \(\{0,1\}\), so Assumption \texttt{ass:bounded-outcomes} holds.  In fact all Bernoulli probabilities lie strictly between zero and one because
\[
 0<p_*\le p_*+g_h(x)\le 3p_*/2\le3/8<1.
\tag{3}
\]
The propensity is the constant \(1/2\), so Assumption \texttt{ass:overlap} follows from \(\kappa<1/2\), and Assumption \texttt{ass:propensity-holder} follows from \(L_\pi\ge1/2\).  The design density is one; hence Assumptions \texttt{ass:global-density-upper} and \texttt{ass:local-density-lower} follow respectively from \(\overline f\ge1\) and \(\underline f\le1\).  The continuous control regression is the constant \(p_*\), whose H\"older norm is \(p_*\le L_\mu/2\), so Assumption \texttt{ass:control-holder} holds.  Finally, consistency gives observed conditional contrasts zero under \(Q_0\) and \(g_h\) under \(Q_h\); (1) therefore verifies Assumption \texttt{ass:cate-holder}.  Definition \texttt{def:full-law-class} now gives
\[
 Q_0,Q_h\in\mathcal P_{\mathrm{full}}.
\tag{4}
\]
By Lemma \texttt{lem:pointwise-identification}, the corresponding causal target values \(\theta_0\) and \(\theta_h\) satisfy
\[
 \theta_0=\tau_{Q_0}^{\mathrm c}(x_0)=0,
 \qquad
 \theta_h=\tau_{Q_h}^{\mathrm c}(x_0)=g_h(x_0)=a_*h^\gamma.
\]
Consequently their separation is
\[
 \Delta_h=|\theta_h-\theta_0|=a_*h^\gamma.
\tag{5}
\]
This is a uniform-design, randomized-treatment, strictly positive regression submodel of the full class; Proposition \texttt{prop:attainable-inclusion} is consistent with, but is not needed to strengthen, the direct membership verification in (4).

Let \(P_0\) and \(P_h\) be the one-record observed laws induced by \(Q_0\) and \(Q_h\).  Relative to Lebesgue measure in \(x\) and counting measure in \((a,y)\), \(P_0\) has density
\[
 p_0(x,a,y)=\frac12p_*^y(1-p_*)^{1-y}.
\]
Only the treated stratum changes under \(P_h\).  Summing over its two possible outcome values gives the exact identities
\[
 \begin{aligned}
 \chi^2(P_h\|P_0)
 &=\frac12\int_{\mathcal X}
   \left\{\frac{g_h(x)^2}{p_*}+\frac{g_h(x)^2}{1-p_*}\right\}\,dx\\
 &=\frac12\int_{\mathcal X}\frac{g_h(x)^2}{p_*(1-p_*)}\,dx
 =C_\chi h^{2\gamma+d},
 \end{aligned}
\tag{6}
\]
where
\[
 C_\chi=\frac{a_*^2}{2p_*(1-p_*)}
 \int_{[-1,1]^d}\varphi(z)^2\,dz<\infty,
\]
and
\[
 \begin{aligned}
 \|P_h-P_0\|_{\mathrm{TV}}
 &=\frac12\int_{\mathcal X}g_h(x)\,dx
 =C_vh^{\gamma+d},\\
 C_v&=\frac{a_*}{2}\int_{[-1,1]^d}\varphi(z)\,dz<\infty.
 \end{aligned}
\tag{7}
\]
The changes of variables in (6)--(7) are exact because the bump support lies inside \(\mathcal X\).

For the privacy-free testing scale, absolute continuity and product factorization give
\[
 1+\chi^2(P_h^n\|P_0^n)
 =\left\{1+\chi^2(P_h\|P_0)\right\}^n.
\tag{8}
\]
Indeed, if \(L_h=dP_h/dP_0\), then independence gives
\[
 \mathbb E_{P_0^n}\left[\left(\prod_{i=1}^nL_h(O_i)\right)^2\right]
 =\prod_{i=1}^n\mathbb E_{P_0}[L_h(O_i)^2],
\]
which is (8).  Cauchy--Schwarz then yields
\[
 \|P_h^n-P_0^n\|_{\mathrm{TV}}
 =\frac12\mathbb E_{P_0^n}\left|\prod_{i=1}^nL_h(O_i)-1\right|
 \le\frac12\sqrt{\chi^2(P_h^n\|P_0^n)}.
\tag{9}
\]
Choose a fixed \(c_1\le r_0\) sufficiently small that
\[
 \exp\{C_\chi c_1^{2\gamma+d}\}-1\le1/16
\]
and set
\[
 h_1=c_1n^{-1/(2\gamma+d)}.
\]
By (6), (8), and \((1+u)^n\le e^{nu}\) for \(u\ge0\),
\[
 \chi^2(P_{h_1}^n\|P_0^n)
 \le \exp\{nC_\chi h_1^{2\gamma+d}\}-1
 =\exp\{C_\chi c_1^{2\gamma+d}\}-1
 \le1/16.
\]
Thus (9) gives \(\|P_{h_1}^n-P_0^n\|_{\mathrm{TV}}\le1/8\).  A Markov kernel contracts total variation: for every output event \(B\),
\[
 \left|\int \mathsf K(z,B)\,d(P_{h_1}^n-P_0^n)(z)\right|
 \le\|P_{h_1}^n-P_0^n\|_{\mathrm{TV}},
\]
because \(0\le\mathsf K(z,B)\le1\).  Taking the supremum over \(B\) proves
\[
 \|P_{h_1}^n\mathsf K-P_0^n\mathsf K\|_{\mathrm{TV}}\le1/8.
\tag{10}
\]

For the privacy scale, put
\[
 w_n=1\wedge(n\epsilon_n)^{-1}.
\]
Choose a fixed \(a_0>0\) so small that \(a_0(e-1+c_0)\le1/8\), and then choose a fixed \(c_2\le r_0\) so small that \(C_vc_2^{\gamma+d}\le a_0\).  Set
\[
 h_2=c_2w_n^{1/(\gamma+d)}.
\]
Equation (7) gives
\[
 \|P_{h_2}-P_0\|_{\mathrm{TV}}
 \le a_0w_n.
\tag{11}
\]
Since \(0<\epsilon_n\le1\), convexity of the exponential on \([0,1]\) gives
\[
 e^{\epsilon_n}-1\le(e-1)\epsilon_n.
\tag{12}
\]
Moreover, the definition of \(w_n\) gives \(nw_n\epsilon_n\le1\), while \(\delta_n\le c_0/n\) and \(w_n\le1\) give \(nw_n\delta_n\le c_0\).  Applying Lemma \texttt{lem:dp-hamming-transport} and then (11)--(12), we obtain
\[
 \begin{aligned}
 \|P_{h_2}^n\mathsf K-P_0^n\mathsf K\|_{\mathrm{TV}}
 &\le n\|P_{h_2}-P_0\|_{\mathrm{TV}}
       (e^{\epsilon_n}-1+\delta_n)\\
 &\le a_0\{(e-1)nw_n\epsilon_n+nw_n\delta_n\}\\
 &\le a_0(e-1+c_0)\le1/8.
 \end{aligned}
\tag{13}
\]

It remains to convert (10) or (13) into an interval-length lower bound.  This conversion is the same for either \(h\in\{h_1,h_2\}\).  Let
\[
 \nu_0=P_0^n\mathsf K,
 \qquad
 \nu_h=P_h^n\mathsf K,
 \qquad
 E_0=\{\theta_0\in\widetilde C_n\},
 \qquad
 E_h=\{\theta_h\in\widetilde C_n\}.
\]
Membership (4) and the assumed honesty give
\[
 \nu_0(E_0)\ge1-\eta,
 \qquad
 \nu_h(E_h)\ge1-\eta.
\tag{14}
\]
Whenever \(\|\nu_h-\nu_0\|_{\mathrm{TV}}\le1/8\), (14) implies
\[
 \begin{aligned}
 \nu_0(E_0\cap E_h)
 &\ge \nu_0(E_0)+\nu_0(E_h)-1\\
 &\ge (1-\eta)+(1-\eta-1/8)-1\\
 &=1-2\eta-1/8>3/8,
 \end{aligned}
\tag{15}
\]
where the strict final inequality uses \(\eta<1/4\).  On \(E_0\cap E_h\), the released interval contains both target values, so its length is at least \(\Delta_h\).  Equations (5) and (15) therefore give
\[
 \mathbb E_{Q_0}[\operatorname{length}(\widetilde C_n)]
 \ge \frac38a_*h^\gamma.
\tag{16}
\]
Using \(h=h_1\) in (16) yields
\[
 \mathbb E_{Q_0}[\operatorname{length}(\widetilde C_n)]
 \ge \frac38a_*c_1^\gamma n^{-\gamma/(2\gamma+d)}.
\tag{17}
\]
Using \(h=h_2\) yields
\[
 \begin{aligned}
 \mathbb E_{Q_0}[\operatorname{length}(\widetilde C_n)]
 &\ge \frac38a_*c_2^\gamma
 w_n^{\gamma/(\gamma+d)}\\
 &=\frac38a_*c_2^\gamma
 \left\{1\wedge(n\epsilon_n)^{-\gamma/(\gamma+d)}\right\}.
 \end{aligned}
\tag{18}
\]
The same null law \(Q_0\) appears in (17) and (18).  Hence its expected length is at least the maximum of the two right-hand sides after replacing their constants by their minimum.  Since \(Q_0\in\mathcal P_{\mathrm{full}}\), taking the supremum over that class proves
\[
 \sup_{Q\in\mathcal P_{\mathrm{full}}}
 \mathbb E_Q[\operatorname{length}(\widetilde C_n)]
 \ge c\left[
 n^{-\gamma/(2\gamma+d)}
 \vee
 \left\{1\wedge(n\epsilon_n)^{-\gamma/(\gamma+d)}\right\}
 \right],
\]
where one may take
\[
 c=\frac38a_*\min\{c_1^\gamma,c_2^\gamma\}>0.
\]
All quantities entering \(c\) are fixed class constants (and allowing dependence on \(\eta\) only weakens the assertion).  The truncation by one in the privacy term is essential for a globally valid statement because every target lies in \([-1,1]\), while the deterministic interval \([-1,1]\) is private and has length two.  The constructed alternatives depend only on the \(\gamma\)-smooth CATE bump, so this proof introduces no \(q<\gamma\) paired-cell branch.
